title: OnDemand CX: Reference Architecture, Private Cloud & Hybrid Resilience
description: Turned an infrastructure capability gap into a productised offering: reference architecture, self-serve pricing and go-to-market. Grew revenue from £500k to £16.6M in 18 months.
context_challenge:
## The problem

Joined an enterprise contact-centre software and services company as Principal Solutions Manager, in a sales and presales role, and later moved into Head of Cloud, on the product side. The job was to support the CTO and represent infrastructure and cloud in front of customers, working alongside the solution architects who built the contact-centre application platform on Avaya's enterprise stack, covering voice, email, web chat and SMS.

At the time, the business only sold Avaya IP Office, aimed at small and medium customers. Avaya Aura, Avaya's enterprise-grade platform, simply wasn't on offer. The private cloud underneath it was built to a mid-market spec, so it couldn't run Aura at enterprise density, and even if it somehow could, the cost would have made it a non-starter.

On top of that, there was no standardised way to scope the infrastructure underneath any of it. The CTO scoped every deal's infrastructure personally, VM sizing, servers, storage and networking, on top of everything else he was responsible for, and being the only person who could do it made him the bottleneck behind the two-week turnaround. Pricing, scoping and handover to the support team varied deal to deal too, since there was no repeatable process behind any of it, just whatever the CTO could get to under pressure. None of that could be fixed with infrastructure alone. It needed a product: something standardised, priced, sellable and repeatable, not dependent on one person's availability.
solution_process:
## The approach

Built a reference architecture that standardised VM configuration and sizing across every design, and tested it until it held up. That alone cut design time from two weeks down to a few days, and freed the CTO from having to personally scope infrastructure for every single deal. On top of it, layered an Excel-based pricing tool with sliders for user counts, front and back office mix, and application selection, so solution architects and salespeople could put together accurate, live pricing with a customer in minutes rather than waiting on a design. It held up too: 100% accurate against the final designs, every time.

Owned this as a product from the start, not just an infrastructure design exercise. Alongside building it, co-led the platform's go-to-market and product management: producing sales material, drafting marketing content for the marketing team to use, and building two tiers of architecture diagram, detailed ones for the solution architects, and simplified, IP-scrubbed versions for customers. Contributed to RFx proposals and sat in on customer meetings directly, treating those conversations as a source of requirements as much as a sales activity. Kept reviewing the architecture in production and fed improvements back in, rather than treating launch as the end point. And ran the cross-functional stakeholder governance, across legal and compliance, support and managed services, and the solution architecture team, that kept priorities aligned across the business as the platform evolved.

The pricing tool wasn't limited to IP Office and Aura either. It was designed to scale across the whole of Avaya's product range, including Oceana, and to price in extra value-add services on top, including line items for Verint and other contact-centre technologies. It could even price an upsell into running a customer's internal IT stack, but that was a deliberate call not to chase. A roadmap is as much about what you don't build as what you do, and running general IT infrastructure wasn't the business's core strength or its unique selling point. What the extensibility work did lead to was a backup-as-a-service and disaster-recovery-as-a-service offer, designed and architected as its own piece of work. That's substantial enough to deserve its own case study, so it isn't covered in detail here.

The reference architecture was built to scope Avaya Aura as well as IP Office, and that's what turned Aura from a market the business had written off into an addressable one, provided a cluster could be built that was both technically capable of running it and commercially viable.

Closed that gap by initiating and negotiating a Dell OEM partnership. That moved the platform onto a standardised, hyperconverged private cloud built on VMware vSAN Ready Nodes, 108 cores per node, virtualising core call-processing infrastructure across dual active-active data centres, with hardened pfSense firewall clusters securing the perimeter. The drop in compute cost was drastic enough to make an enterprise-capable private cloud commercially viable, and that's what turned the Aura opportunity into a live, sellable segment for the business.

The application platform itself, owned by the solution architecture team, evolved over time: from siloed multi-channel routing, to true omnichannel, and eventually to Avaya Oceana's unified desktop. Every time it shipped a new evolution, the infrastructure and middleware layer underneath had to keep pace, along with the reference architecture and pricing model, and that's the part this role owned.

Worked with the support and managed service team to optimise the platform's centralised monitoring stack, Prometheus and Grafana, and helped standardise endpoint and server security through Sophos Enterprise, and backup through Veeam Backup & Replication, across the platform. Separately, wrote a technical and commercial proposal to replace the legacy pfSense perimeter with VMware NSX and Darktrace's AI-driven threat detection. The executive team liked it on technical merit, but it got deferred on budget.

Also designed a hybrid resilience layer for the platform, using AWS as a standby site for active and passive disaster recovery, since that's where Avaya's platform components were actually supported. Scoped an equivalent design on Azure too, using infrastructure-as-a-service and native cloud services, but it never got implemented. Avaya just didn't support it there at the time.
artifacts_deliverables:
## Deliverables

- Standardised infrastructure reference architecture and self-serve Excel pricing tool, scoped across the full Avaya product range (IP Office, Aura and Oceana) plus third-party add-ons such as Verint
- Backup-as-a-Service and DR-as-a-Service offer, designed and architected off the back of the pricing tool's extensibility (its own case study covers this in detail)
- Two-tier architecture diagrams: detailed versions for solution architects, IP-scrubbed high-level versions for customers
- Sales and marketing content, plus input into RFx proposals and direct customer meetings
- Ongoing stakeholder governance across legal/compliance, support and managed services, and the solution architecture team
- Dell OEM hyperconverged private cloud on VMware vSAN Ready Nodes, dual active-active data centres
- Hardened pfSense firewall clusters
- Monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) and security/backup standardisation (Sophos Enterprise, Veeam B&R), delivered with the support and managed service team
- Technical/commercial proposal for VMware NSX + Darktrace (accepted on merit, deferred on budget)
- AWS standby site for active/passive disaster recovery
- Azure resilience design scoped (IaaS and native services), not implemented as Avaya did not support it at the time
outcome_impact:
## Results

- Identified and opened the enterprise Avaya Aura market for the business, a segment it had never been able to serve. 16 of the platform's 28 live customers are on Aura now, up from zero
- Solution design time: 2 weeks → a few days
- Customer pricing turnaround: 2 weeks → minutes, self-serve by sales
- 100% pricing accuracy validated against final designs
- ~50% reduction in server footprint and cost via the Dell OEM partnership, with ~66% more raw compute capacity per node, and roughly 2 to 3x usable compute density once virtualised and consolidated
- 99.999% platform availability maintained across the dual active-active private cloud deployment
- Revenue growth: £500k → £16.6M in 18 months
